sections.h2: Can a squatter in West Virginia ever become the legal owner?
sections.html:
Yes, but only by meeting a long list of requirements for a full ten years. West Virginia does not have a short squatter statute. A person who occupies land and claims title relies on the doctrine of adverse possession, and the courts hold that person to a heavy burden of proof.

Ten years comes from W. Va. Code 55-2-1, which says no one may make an entry on land or bring an action to recover it except within ten years after the right first accrued to that person or to someone through whom they claim. When an owner waits too long to act against an occupant, the clock can matter. This page explains how the doctrine works, how it differs from a tenant who stays after a lease, and what an owner selling a house can do.

sections.h2: What must an adverse possessor prove?
sections.html:
The West Virginia Supreme Court of Appeals lists six elements. One who seeks title to a tract by adverse possession must prove each of them for the statutory period (Somon v. Murphy Fabrication & Erection Co., 160 W.Va. 84, 232 S.E.2d 524 (1977), repeated in Elder v. Smith (1996)).

  1. The land was held adversely or hostilely.
  2. The possession was actual.
  3. It was open and notorious, sometimes stated as visible and notorious.
  4. It was exclusive.
  5. It was continuous.
  6. It was under claim of title or color of title.

The statutory period is ten years. Missing any element defeats the claim.

The burden is also stricter than in an ordinary civil case. In Cobb v. Collins (2018), the Court repeated that the party claiming title by adverse possession must prove all essential elements by clear and convincing evidence, citing Brown v. Brown, 196 W.Va. 559, 474 S.E.2d 489 (1996).

sections.h2: What does "hostile" mean when someone occupies land?
sections.html:
Hostile means against the owner's right, not angry. In Elder v. Smith the Court explained that the claimant must show possession against the right of the true owner and inconsistent with the owner's title. The Court added that the word hostile is synonymous with adverse and does not require ill will or malevolence toward the owner.

That matters for an owner who gave permission. Someone staying in a relative's house with the owner's consent, or paying rent as a tenant, is not holding against the owner's right in the way the doctrine requires.

If a claimant does satisfy every element for more than ten years, the Court's syllabus point quoted in Cobb says actual, open, notorious, exclusive and continuous adverse possession for more than ten years confers good legal title, enabling the owner to maintain an action for unlawful entry and detainer against one who enters unlawfully (Harman v. Alt, 69 W.Va. 287, 71 S.E. 709 (1911)).

sections.h2: What is the difference between a squatter and a holdover tenant?
sections.html:
A tenant entered with the owner's permission under a lease or oral arrangement, so the landlord-tenant statutes apply. A squatter entered with no right at all. The remedies differ.

SituationMain legal routeSource
Tenant behind on rent, in breach, or damaging the propertyVerified petition in magistrate or circuit court; hearing 5 to 10 judicial days after filingW. Va. Code 55-3A-1
Occupant claiming title by long possessionAdverse possession doctrine; six elements, ten years, clear and convincing proof55-2-1; Somon; Cobb
Person on property without authority after being asked to leaveCriminal trespass in a structure: misdemeanor, fine up to $10061-3B-2(a)
Entering a structure posted as condemnedMisdemeanor, fine up to $100, jail up to six months, or both61-3B-2(b)

The summary route in Article 3A is written for tenants. It lets a person desiring to remove a tenant apply to the court, and a tenant who is served may raise any defense available in an ejectment or unlawful detainer action (55-3A-2). Whether a particular occupant is a tenant, a guest or a trespasser is a fact question, so get legal advice before acting.

sections.h2: What does West Virginia law say about trespass on a house?
sections.html:
Under W. Va. Code 61-3B-2(a), a person who knowingly enters a structure without being authorized, licensed or invited, or who is asked to leave by the owner, tenant or agent and refuses, is guilty of a misdemeanor, with a fine of not more than $100.

Subsection (b) is stronger for condemned buildings: a person who knowingly and willfully enters a structure with a clear posting that a municipal or county government has condemned it as unfit for human habitation faces a fine of not more than $100, up to six months in jail, or both. For a first violation the court may substitute community service or pretrial diversion. Subsection (c) carries heavier penalties when the offender is armed with a dangerous weapon and intends bodily injury.

A separate section, 61-3B-3, covers trespass on property other than a structure where notice against entering is given. The details depend on how notice is given, so read the section itself before posting land.

sections.h2: What should an owner do about an unauthorized occupant?
sections.html:
Act early, in writing, and through the proper channel. We are not lawyers, and the right step depends on whether the person is a tenant, a guest, or someone with no connection to you. These are practical points that follow from the statutes above.

  • Document when you last inspected the house and who had permission to be there.
  • If the person is asked to leave and refuses, the trespass statute refers to a request by the owner, tenant or agent, so keep a record of that request.
  • If the person paid or promised rent, treat the matter as a tenancy and use the Article 3A petition rather than self-help.
  • Do not wait years. Section 55-2-1 gives ten years for an action to recover land, and the adverse possession elements include continuous possession.
  • Talk to a West Virginia attorney before changing locks, shutting off utilities or removing belongings.

Vacant inherited houses are a common setup for these problems. A house sits empty after a death, the owner lives out of state, and months pass between visits. Checking the property regularly, keeping the taxes current and recording who holds title all make it harder for anyone to claim they were there openly and exclusively.

sections.h2: How does an occupant problem affect selling a West Virginia house?
sections.html:
It affects who can close and how fast. A buyer who plans to live in the house needs possession at closing. A traditional buyer with a mortgage will also have an appraiser and an inspector who need access, and a contested occupant can stall both.

If you own a house with a squatter, a holdover tenant or an unclear occupancy, you can still sell. We buy houses in West Virginia as-is, and we can discuss an offer on a property where someone is living without your agreement. We will not tell you the occupant has no rights, and you should not rely on us for that answer. The title question belongs to a court, and the practical timeline depends on which statute applies.

Before you list or accept an offer, assemble what you can: the deed, tax bills, any lease, texts or letters with the occupant, and photos showing the condition and date. These help whether you evict, negotiate a move-out or sell with the occupant in place.

faqs.q: How long does adverse possession take in West Virginia?
faqs.a: Ten years. W. Va. Code 55-2-1 sets ten years for entering on or recovering land, and the Supreme Court of Appeals lists ten years as the statutory period for adverse possession. The claimant must also prove each of the six elements.

faqs.q: What standard of proof applies to an adverse possession claim?
faqs.a: Clear and convincing evidence. In Cobb v. Collins (2018) the Court repeated that the party claiming title by adverse possession bears the burden of proving all essential elements by clear and convincing evidence.

faqs.q: Does a squatter have to be hostile to the owner?
faqs.a: Hostile means possession against the owner's right and inconsistent with the owner's title. The Court said it does not require ill will or malevolence. Someone who has the owner's permission is not occupying against the owner's right in that sense.

faqs.q: Is trespassing in a house a crime in West Virginia?
faqs.a: Yes. Under 61-3B-2(a), knowingly entering a structure without authorization, or refusing to leave after being asked, is a misdemeanor punishable by a fine of not more than $100. Entering a structure posted as condemned carries a higher penalty.

faqs.q: Can I sell my house if someone is living there without permission?
faqs.a: You can sell the property, but possession is the practical issue. A buyer who needs to move in will want the occupant gone. A cash buyer who purchases as-is may be willing to take a house with an occupant, so ask for an offer and describe the situation honestly.
